_citation: Mallama, A. & Hilton, J. L. (2018), 'Computing apparent planetary magnitudes for The Astronomical Almanac', Astronomy and Computing 25, 10-24. DOI:10.1016/j.ascom.2018.08.002 (preprint arXiv:1808.01973, revised 2018 June 21).
_transcription: Equations 2-17 of the paper (Sec. 3), transcribed by hand. The authors' reference implementation Ap_Mag_V3.f90 (https://sourceforge.net/projects/planetary-magnitudes/, folder Ap_Mag_Current_Version) is downloaded by the light stage and every coefficient below is checked to appear verbatim in it (tests/test_photometry_phase.py).
_form: V(alpha) = 5 log10(r d) + const + sum_i coeffs[i] * alpha^i ('poly', alpha in degrees), or const - 2.5 log10(sum_i coeffs[i] * (alpha/180)^i) ('logpoly180'). Pieces apply on (min_deg, max_deg].

199.name: Mercury
199.V10_zero_phase_note: Sec. 3.1: the polynomial's zeroth-order term (-0.613) is ~8% fainter than the geophysical (opposition-surge) model value -0.694 of Mallama et al. (2002, 2017); the polynomial is fit to 2 < alpha < 170 deg.

399.name: Earth
399.V10_zero_phase_note: Sec. 3.3: V1(0) from Mallama et al. (2017), synthetic photometry of EPOXI spectrophotometry (Livengood et al. 2011); phase curve is a spline fit to the 'realistic clouds' model of Tinetti et al. (2006), i.e. a model, not an observation.

499.name: Mars
499.V10_zero_phase_note: Sec. 3.4: plus L(lambda_e) (sub-longitude, rms 0.035 mag) and L(Ls) (season) corrections from Mallama (2007), not represented here.

pieces.note: Beyond 50 deg no observations exist; the authors approximate Mars by averaging the Mercury and Earth curves.
Cassini ISS green-filter phase curve of Mayorga et al. (2016); constant adjusted for continuity at 12 deg.

699.name: Saturn (globe without rings)
699.V10_zero_phase_note: Sec. 3.6: globe-alone V1(0) from synthetic photometry of Karkoschka (1998) at the 1995 ring-plane crossing (Mallama & Pavlov 2017).

pieces.note: The globe's curve at alpha < 6.5 deg adopts Jupiter's second-order polynomial (Eq. 8) combined with Saturn's synthetic V1(0).

Fourth-order fit to the red-light phase function digitized from the Pioneer-based model of Dyudina et al. (2005, Fig. 7). The paper prints -1.505E-6 for the cubic term; Ap_Mag_V3.f90 uses -1.506e-6 (<= 0.004 mag difference at 150 deg). The paper's value is used.

rings_eq10.note: Globe + rings, used only to compare with JPL Horizons (which includes the rings for alpha < 6.5 deg and effective inclination < 27 deg).

799.name: Uranus
799.V10_zero_phase_note: Eq. 14/15: V1(0) = -7.110 - 8.4e-4 phi', phi' = mean of |planetographic sub-Earth latitude| and |sub-solar latitude| (deg). In Ap_Mag_V3.f90 the phase term is applied only above the geocentric limit alpha = 3.1 deg.

899.name: Neptune
899.V10_zero_phase_note: Eq. 16 for t > 2000.0. In Ap_Mag_V3.f90 the phase term (Eq. 17) is applied only above the geocentric limit alpha = 1.9 deg.
